protocol.instrument_name: Protocol for Management of Mild Acne
protocol.legal_basis: Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act 1981 (Vic) and Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Regulations 2017 (Vic); requirement of the Secretary Approval: Community Pharmacist Program to comply with this Protocol when supplying Schedule 4 poisons for patients seeking treatment for mild acne under a structured prescribing arrangement (p.4).
protocol.supervision_model: Structured prescribing arrangement: pharmacists authorised under the Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Regulations 2017 supply the Schedule 4 poisons documented in the Protocol; must have completed the designated pharmacist training course before supplying Schedule 4 poisons; must operate in accordance with the Act, the Regulations and the Pharmacy Board of Australia Code of Conduct (p.4).
protocol.scope_summary: Victorian Community Pharmacist Program protocol authorising supply of specified topical medicines (topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide combinations, topical clindamycin) for mild acne in patients aged 12 years and over, with triage/exclusion flowcharts, an initiate-treatment flowchart, a review flowchart, and a maximum 6-week supply limit. Supplementary information (patient history, examination, severity table, general measures, medicines, communication and follow-up) supports the flowcharts.

Does the patient/parent/caregiver consent to participate in the Program? (Yes required; * The patient must be physically present at the pharmacy)

Examination confirms that the patient has mild acne; comedones +/- pustules and papules must be present (refer to images in resources such as the Therapeutic Guidelines and DermNet NZ; consider differential diagnoses e.g. folliculitis, rosacea, acneiform eruptions).
Does the patient meet any of the following exclusion criteria? answer must be 'No, to all' in order to Proceed

exclusion.text: Unable to make a clear diagnosis of mild acne
Acne is painful, severe, cystic or scarring, acne excoriee is present, or the patient has a family history of scarring acne (note: even persistent mild acne can scar)

Patient is pregnant or planning pregnancy, as there are medicines in this protocol which are schedule D (definition p.4: 'Planning pregnancy: Actively trying to conceive or intending to conceive in the next 1-3 months.')
The patient is taking a medicine that can cause or aggravate acne
A female patient has PMOS/PCOS, or presents with signs of androgenisation (i.e. hirsutism, obesity and/or menstrual irregularity)
Acne has worsened, repeatedly relapsed, or not responded despite use of appropriate topical treatment
Topical treatments within this protocol have been poorly tolerated

steps.description: Patient history: Review MHR, where possible/available; Onset, duration, nature, location, and severity of lesions; Medical history (e.g. PMOS/PCOS); Pregnancy and lactation status, including planning to become pregnant; Hormone changes and signs of androgenisation in women (e.g. hirsutism, obesity, and menstrual irregularity); Current and recently commenced medications, including topical products; Medication allergies, adverse effects, and/or sensitivities to medicines (and other topical products); Current management strategies for acne, including hygiene, skin care regimens, and products; Response to prior treatment or management strategies; Aggravating factors (e.g. occupation and exposure to comedogenic factors); Emotional and social impacts of acne; History of eczema or sensitive skin, as topical agents for acne can be irritating.

Examination: 'Confirm that the patient has mild acne; comedones +/- pustules and papules must be present. Refer to images in resources such as the Therapeutic Guidelines and DermNet NZ. Consider differential diagnoses (e.g. folliculitis, rosacea, acneiform eruptions).'

gates.criterion: Comedones +/- pustules and papules present and a clear diagnosis of mild acne can be made

steps.description: 'Does the patient meet any of the following exclusion criteria?' (EXC-1 to EXC-7, page 7). 'Yes, to any' -> 'Refer to General Practitioner for treatment'. 'No, to all' -> 'Proceed'.

gates.criterion: Patient meets none of the exclusion criteria EXC-1 to EXC-7

AND/OR: The condition is having a marked negative emotional and social effect on the patient (quality of life is significantly affected)' - Yes -> 'Refer to General Practitioner for immediate review and follow up' (treatment may still be provided per page 15). No -> continue to PW-1-S10.

gates.criterion: The condition is having a marked negative emotional and social effect on the patient (quality of life is significantly affected)

steps.description: 'Has the patient been using OTC acne treatment without sufficient clinical improvement, or relapsed after initial response?' Yes -> 'Refer to A. Initiate Mild Acne Treatment Flowchart' (PW-2). No -> continue to PW-1-S11.

gates.criterion: Patient has been using OTC acne treatment without sufficient clinical improvement, or relapsed after initial response

steps.description: 'Has the patient previously used a topical acne treatment on the Medicines List and relapsed after initial response?' Yes -> 'Refer to A. Initiate Mild Acne Treatment Flowchart' (PW-2). No -> continue to PW-1-S12.

gates.criterion: Patient has previously used a topical acne treatment on the Medicines List and relapsed after initial response

steps.description: 'Has the patient been using a topical acne treatment on the Medicines List continuously for the past 6 weeks*, requiring review?' Yes -> 'Refer to B. Review of Mild Acne Treatment Flowchart' (PW-3). No -> 'IF NO TO ALL, REFER TO A GENERAL PRACTITIONER.' Footnote: '* It is recommended that acne treatments are reviewed for efficacy after 6 weeks, but continued for at least 3-4 months, of daily use before being labelled as not effective. Treatment failure is most often associated with issues with adherence and incorrect use. Treatments may be supplied as part of the Program or from a medical practitioner.'

gates.criterion: Patient has been using a topical acne treatment on the Medicines List continuously for the past 6 weeks and requiring review

diagnosis_pathways.name: A. INITIATE MILD ACNE TREATMENT FLOWCHART (pages 8-9)

steps.description: Identify the dominant type of acne present: (A) Mainly comedonal with minimal inflammation; (B) Mainly comedonal, with some inflammatory papules and pustules; (C) Mainly inflammatory papules and pustules, with some comedones; (D) Mix of both comedonal and inflammatory papules and pustules.

provenance.section_heading: A. INITIATE MILD ACNE TREATMENT FLOWCHART

steps.description: Choose a topical treatment option according to the dominant type of acne present (refer to Medicines List for full product details). A) Mainly comedonal with minimal inflammation -> Topical retinoid: adapalene 0.1% OR tretinoin 0.05% OR trifarotene 0.005%. B) Mainly comedonal with some inflammatory papules and pustules -> Topical combination of retinoid (low strength) and benzoyl peroxide: adapalene 0.1% + benzoyl peroxide 2.5%. C) Mainly inflammatory papules and pustules with some comedones -> Topical combination of antibiotic and benzoyl peroxide: First-line: clindamycin 1% + benzoyl peroxide 5% OR Second-line: single agent topical clindamycin 1%*. D) Mix of both comedonal and inflammatory papules and pustules -> Topical combination of antibiotic and retinoid: First-line: clindamycin 1% + tretinoin 0.025% OR Second-line: single agent topical clindamycin 1%*. '*Topical clindamycin as a single agent preparation should only be supplied if the patient's skin is prone to irritation (e.g. patients with atopic skin conditions).'

provenance.section_heading: A. INITIATE MILD ACNE TREATMENT FLOWCHART

steps.description: Confirm management plan is appropriate with regards to contraindications, precautions, interactions, pregnancy and lactation status. 'Treatments under this protocol are NOT appropriate' -> 'Refer to General Practitioner'. 'Treatments under this protocol are appropriate' -> continue to pg. 9. 'If a topical retinoid is being provided to a female of child-bearing age, the pharmacist must provide comprehensive contraceptive counselling.'

gates.criterion: Management plan is appropriate with regards to contraindications, precautions, interactions, pregnancy and lactation status

provenance.section_heading: A. INITIATE MILD ACNE TREATMENT FLOWCHART

steps.description: Dispense medications via pharmacy dispensing software and label according to legislative requirements outlined in the Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Regulation 2017. 'Supply is limited to a maximum of 6 weeks of the appropriate medication.'

Communicate agreed treatment plan to patient and other healthcare professionals: Provide education about general measures for acne; Advise patient to review treatment in 6 weeks with medical practitioner or pharmacist (Patient should be advised to return for earlier follow up if required (i.e. intolerance to treatment)); Provide a patient handout outlining consultation and remind patient to present this at their next follow-up/review with the pharmacist or medical practitioner.
Document the consultation and share a record of the service with the patient and patient's usual treating general practitioner or medical practice where the patient has one.

diagnosis_pathways.name: B. REVIEW OF MILD ACNE TREATMENT FLOWCHART (pages 10-11)

steps.description: Assess the effectiveness and tolerance of topical treatment after at least 6 weeks of continuous use to determine if treatment should be resupplied or changed.

provenance.section_heading: B. REVIEW OF MILD ACNE TREATMENT FLOWCHART

steps.description: Branch on treatment response for each existing topical treatment (rows A-F): 'Action if acne is improving' (-> PW-3-S3) versus 'Action if treatment is not sufficiently effective' (-> PW-3-S4).

gates.criterion: Acne is improving after at least 6 weeks of continuous use of the existing topical treatment

provenance.section_heading: B. REVIEW OF MILD ACNE TREATMENT FLOWCHART

steps.description: Action if acne is improving, by existing topical treatment: A. Topical retinoid (adapalene 0.1% OR tretinoin 0.05% OR trifarotene 0.005%) -> 'Resupply topical retinoid for maintenance. Reduce frequency of treatment if acne is resolving.' B. Topical combination of retinoid (low strength) and benzoyl peroxide (adapalene 0.1% + benzoyl peroxide 2.5%) -> 'Switch to topical retinoid for maintenance: adapalene 0.1% OR tretinoin 0.05% OR trifarotene 0.005%.' C. Topical combination of retinoid (high strength) and benzoyl peroxide (adapalene 0.3% + benzoyl peroxide 2.5%) -> 'Switch to topical retinoid for maintenance: adapalene 0.1% OR tretinoin 0.05% OR trifarotene 0.005%.' D. Topical combination of antibiotic and benzoyl peroxide (clindamycin 1% + benzoyl peroxide 5%*) -> 'Resupply clindamycin 1% + benzoyl peroxide 5%*, OR Switch to benzoyl peroxide (OTC) for maintenance if inflammation has resolved.' E. Topical combination of antibiotic and retinoid (clindamycin 1% + tretinoin 0.025%*) -> 'Resupply clindamycin 1% + tretinoin 0.025%*, OR Switch to topical retinoid for maintenance if inflammation has resolved: adapalene 0.1% OR tretinoin 0.05% OR trifarotene 0.005%.' F. Topical antibiotic (clindamycin 1%*) -> 'Resupply clindamycin 1%*, OR Stop treatment, if inflammation has resolved.' Footnote: '*Topical clindamycin should be stopped if inflammation has resolved or limited to a total of 3 months of continuous treatment. Refer to GP if inflammation has not sufficiently resolved after 3 months treatment with topical clindamycin.'

provenance.section_heading: B. REVIEW OF MILD ACNE TREATMENT FLOWCHART

steps.description: Action if treatment is not sufficiently effective, by existing topical treatment: A. Topical retinoid -> 'Therapies guided by dominant type of acne: If acne is mainly comedonal with some inflammatory papules and pustules, switch to adapalene 0.1% + benzoyl peroxide 2.5%, OR If acne is a mix of both comedonal and inflammatory papules and pustules, switch to clindamycin 1% + tretinoin 0.025%*, OR Refer to General Practitioner.' B. Topical combination of retinoid (low strength) and benzoyl peroxide -> 'Switch to topical combination of retinoid (high strength) and benzoyl peroxide: adapalene 0.3% + benzoyl peroxide 2.5%.' C. Topical combination of retinoid (high strength) and benzoyl peroxide -> 'Refer to General Practitioner.' D. Topical combination of antibiotic and benzoyl peroxide -> 'Refer to General Practitioner.' E. Topical combination of antibiotic and retinoid -> 'Refer to General Practitioner.' F. Topical antibiotic -> 'Refer to General Practitioner.'

treatments.quantity_to_supply: Supply is limited to a maximum of 6 weeks of the appropriate medication
treatments.notes: Brand name example: Differin. NB1: Cream formulations are preferred for patients with dry or sensitive skin. Gel formulations are preferred for those with oily skin. NB2: Adapalene is available as a Schedule 3 formulation. NB3: For patients starting topical retinoids, introduce these gradually because they can irritate the skin initially. E.g. Apply to affected area(s) for 2 hours for the first 2 nights, then increase to alternate nights for the first 2 weeks, then once daily at night as tolerated. Topical retinoids are potentially teratogenic and should be avoided in patients who are planning to become pregnancy or who are pregnant (p.17). Listed as option A (mainly comedonal with minimal inflammation) in the Initiate flowchart; also used for maintenance in the Review flowchart.

treatments.quantity_to_supply: Supply is limited to a maximum of 6 weeks of the appropriate medication
treatments.notes: Brand name example: Retrieve. NB1: Cream formulations are preferred for patients with dry or sensitive skin. NB3: For patients starting topical retinoids, introduce these gradually because they can irritate the skin initially. E.g. Apply to affected area(s) for 2 hours for the first 2 nights, then increase to alternate nights for the first 2 weeks, then once daily at night as tolerated. Topical retinoids are potentially teratogenic and should be avoided in patients who are planning to become pregnancy or who are pregnant (p.17).

Apply to affected area(s) for 2 hours for the first 2 nights, then increase to alternate nights for the first 2 weeks, then once daily at night as tolerated. Topical retinoids are potentially teratogenic and should be avoided in patients who are planning to become pregnancy or who are pregnant (p.17).

treatments.quantity_to_supply: Supply is limited to a maximum of 6 weeks of the appropriate medication
treatments.notes: Brand name examples: Epiduo, Epiduo Forte. Class: Topical retinoid and antibacterial. NB4: Benzoyl peroxide can stain pillows and clothing as per Product Information. NB3 gradual introduction of retinoid applies. Used as the option for dominant type B (mainly comedonal with some inflammatory papules and pustules).

treatments.quantity_to_supply: Supply is limited to a maximum of 6 weeks of the appropriate medication
treatments.notes: High-strength retinoid combination listed in the Medicines table; brand name examples Epiduo, Epiduo Forte. Used in the Review flowchart when treatment with the low-strength combination (adapalene 0.1% + benzoyl peroxide 2.5%) is not sufficiently effective ('Switch to topical combination of retinoid (high strength) and benzoyl peroxide: adapalene 0.3% + benzoyl peroxide 2.5%', p.10). NB4: Benzoyl peroxide can stain pillows and clothing as per Product Information.

treatments.quantity_to_supply: Supply is limited to a maximum of 6 weeks of the appropriate medication
treatments.notes: Brand name example: Duac Once Daily. Class: Topical antibiotic and antibacterial. Initiate flowchart (dominant type C, mainly inflammatory papules and pustules with some comedones): 'First-line: clindamycin 1% + benzoyl peroxide 5%'. NB4: Benzoyl peroxide can stain pillows and clothing as per Product Information. Topical clindamycin use limited to a total of 3 months; discontinue when inflammatory lesions have adequately resolved (p.17, p.20).

treatments.quantity_to_supply: Supply is limited to a maximum of 6 weeks of the appropriate medication
treatments.notes: Brand name example: Acnatac. Class: Topical antibiotic and retinoid. Initiate flowchart (dominant type D, mix of both comedonal and inflammatory papules and pustules): 'First-line: clindamycin 1% + tretinoin 0.025%'. NB3 gradual introduction of retinoid applies. Topical clindamycin use limited to a total of 3 months; discontinue when inflammatory lesions have adequately resolved (p.17, p.20).

treatments.quantity_to_supply: Supply is limited to a maximum of 6 weeks of the appropriate medication
treatments.notes: Single-agent topical clindamycin. 'Topical clindamycin as a single agent preparation should only be supplied if the patient's skin is prone to irritation (e.g. patients with atopic skin conditions)' (p.8); 'Use of topical clindamycin should be limited to a total of 3 months to limit development of resistance. Topical clindamycin should be discontinued when inflammatory lesions have adequately resolved, but may be resumed if inflammation recurs' (p.17). Second-line option for dominant types C and D in the Initiate flowchart.

Maintenance option in the Review flowchart only: 'Switch to benzoyl peroxide (OTC) for maintenance if inflammation has resolved' (row D, action if acne is improving, p.10). No strength, dose or frequency is printed for this maintenance step in the document; full product details are referred to the Medicines List.

review_followup.what: Advise patient to review treatment in 6 weeks with medical practitioner or pharmacist. Patient should be advised to return for earlier follow up if required (i.e. intolerance to treatment).

Topical treatment for mild acne should be reviewed every 6 weeks to assess effectiveness and tolerance to treatment. Earlier review can be considered especially if the patient is unable to tolerate treatment (i.e. sensitivity or reaction). Where feasible, follow-up reviews should be conducted by the same pharmacist to enable continuity of care and consistent evaluation of treatment response, progress, and potential treatment failure.

review_followup.when: After 6 weeks of daily use (before labelling treatment not effective)
review_followup.what: It is recommended that acne treatments are reviewed for efficacy after 6 weeks, but continued for at least 3-4 months, of daily use before being labelled as not effective. Treatment failure is most often associated with issues with adherence and incorrect use.

review_followup.when: Total of 3 months of continuous topical clindamycin treatment
review_followup.what: The use of topical antibiotics (e.g. topical clindamycin) should be limited to a total of 3 months to limit development of resistance. Topical clindamycin should be discontinued when inflammatory lesions have adequately resolved, but may be resumed if inflammation recurs, with regular review for ongoing need.

review_followup.when: Once papular inflammation has resolved or inflammatory acne is under control
review_followup.what: Patients should be changed to maintenance treatment with single agent (e.g. topical retinoid or benzoyl peroxide).

conditions: The pharmacist must share a copy of the record of the service with the patient and with the patient's usual treating medical practitioner or medical practice, where the patient has one.
The pharmacist must make a record in the pharmacy software and an IT system approved by the Victorian Department of Health, regarding the supply.

hugh_to_confirm.item: 'Where the protocol indicates to "Refer to General Practitioner," the Pharmacist may refer to a medical practitioner or other authorised prescribing health practitioner as clinically appropriate' - confirm which referral destinations are accepted locally.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Referral destination flexibility is left to clinical judgement; local policy must define acceptable recipients before go-live.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Requirement that pharmacists have completed the designated pharmacist training course before supplying Schedule 4 poisons.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Eligibility to use the protocol depends on a training-completion record that must be verified per pharmacist.

hugh_to_confirm.item: 'Pharmacists are also expected to exercise professional judgment in adapting treatment guidelines to presenting circumstances.'
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Open-ended professional judgement clause needs a local policy boundary for an automated rules engine.

hugh_to_confirm.item: 'Review MHR, where possible/available' during patient history.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Depends on local system access and patient consent arrangements.

hugh_to_confirm.item: 'Topical clindamycin as a single agent preparation should only be supplied if the patient's skin is prone to irritation (e.g. patients with atopic skin conditions).'
hugh_to_confirm.reason: 'Prone to irritation' is a judgement criterion not numerically defined by the document; needs local policy definition.

hugh_to_confirm.item: 'If a topical retinoid is being provided to a female of child-bearing age, the pharmacist must provide comprehensive contraceptive counselling' and 'A referral to medical practitioner should concurrently be made for initiation of contraception with prescription medication if requested'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Counselling content and the 'if requested' referral trigger are left to local policy.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Sharing the record of the service with the patient's usual treating general practitioner 'where the patient has one'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Local process for identifying the usual GP and sharing records must be confirmed.

hugh_to_confirm.item: NB3 graduated topical retinoid introduction is printed as an example ('E.g. Apply to affected area(s) for 2 hours for the first 2 nights, then increase to alternate nights for the first 2 weeks, then once daily at night as tolerated').
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Example regimen, not a mandatory schedule; confirm the counselling wording to be used in the product.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Supply limited to a maximum of 6 weeks of the appropriate medication, dispensed via pharmacy dispensing software and labelled per the Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Regulation 2017.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Quantity/dispensing implementation must be configured in local dispensing software.
